lesson.title: The Square Deal: Roosevelt's Promise of Fair Treatment for Labor, Business, and Consumers
lesson.summary: Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal was his domestic reform program, resting on what he called the three Cs, control of corporations, consumer protection, and conservation, and it was first tested when Roosevelt broke precedent to intervene in the 1902 anthracite coal strike as a neutral arbiter rather than siding automatically with business.
lesson.body:
By the time Theodore Roosevelt became president in 1901, the labor movement had spent decades organizing against dangerous conditions, low wages, and long hours in America's mines, mills, and factories, usually facing a federal government that treated labor unrest as a threat to order rather than a legitimate grievance. Roosevelt's Square Deal, the label attached to his domestic program, promised something different: a government that would act as an honest broker between labor, business, and the public rather than an automatic ally of capital. Roosevelt summarized his approach as resting on three Cs, control of corporations, consumer protection, and conservation of natural resources, and the name Square Deal itself was meant to convey fairness to all sides rather than favoritism toward any one.

The clearest early test of this philosophy came in 1902, when roughly 150,000 anthracite coal miners in Pennsylvania went on strike, organized by the United Mine Workers under John Mitchell, demanding higher wages, shorter hours, and recognition of their union. As autumn approached and coal supplies for heating homes and schools ran short, the crisis threatened real hardship across the Northeast. Previous presidents faced with major strikes, most notably Grover Cleveland during the 1894 Pullman Strike, had generally sided with owners and used federal troops to break the strike. Roosevelt instead summoned both the mine owners and union leaders to the White House, an unprecedented step, and when the owners refused to negotiate, he threatened to have the Army seize and operate the mines itself. That pressure forced the owners to accept arbitration by a commission Roosevelt appointed, which ultimately granted the miners a wage increase and a shorter workday, though it stopped short of recognizing the union itself.

The coal strike settlement did not satisfy everyone, and it did not resolve the underlying tension between capital and labor, but it established something new: a president willing to treat organized labor as a legitimate party at the table rather than a threat to be suppressed, while still working within the system rather than simply dictating terms to business. That balancing act, intervening enough to prevent one side from steamrolling the other without becoming labor's uncritical ally, became the template for the rest of Roosevelt's domestic agenda, from his antitrust suits against corporations to his consumer protection laws to his conservation program, all extensions of the same basic promise that government would referee fairly rather than simply protect entrenched power.
